title: The third jhana
hookLine: lotuses under water, soaked from root to tip (MN 39)

cards: In a lotus pond, most of the flowers rise up and open on the surface, where everyone can see them. Those are the ones on the postcards. But some never come up.
They sprout under water, grow under water, and stay there, cool water all around them from the roots to the tips of the petals. You'd walk right past them. Nothing about them is showy.

teach.h: THE JOY FADES; THE EASE STAYS.
teach.b: Here is how MN 39 describes the third jhana.

With the fading away of joy, a person abides in equanimity, mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, and enters the third jhana, of which the noble ones say: one who is equanimous and mindful dwells in pleasure.
Then the picture. In a pond of blue, red or white lotuses, some are born and grow in the water and thrive immersed, never rising out, and cool water soaks them from their tips to their roots.
That's how this quiet pleasure fills the body. What changes from yesterday? Two Pali words help.
Piti is joy with a bubble in it: rapture, excitement, the child on the morning of a trip. Sukha is pleasure without the bubble: contentment, the grandmother on the porch.
In the third jhana, piti fades and sukha stays, and a new quality comes forward: upekkha, equanimity, looking on evenly.
Many centuries later, the Visuddhimagga, a Theravada meditation manual, gives an image for the difference.
A traveler worn out in the desert hears that there's a pond at the edge of a wood: that thrill is piti.

Then he reaches it, drinks and rests in the shade: that's sukha. The third jhana is happiness that no longer needs to rise and be seen; the mind stays mindful and fully aware, and the ease simply soaks through.

how: In Theravada meditation teaching the jhanas are usually described in this order, with the fading of rapture and the growth of equanimity marking the third; the lotus is a common Buddhist image in art and teaching across schools.

o: not caring what happens to anyone

games.q: match the words of the third jhana.

s: the third jhana is more excited than the second
the bubbling joy fades; quiet ease and equanimity remain.
the noble ones say the equanimous and mindful dwell in pleasure
that's the text's own description of the third jhana.
the lotuses in the simile rise to bloom on the surface
they thrive under water, soaked from tip to root.

games.q: the bubbling joy of the second jhana fades away. what's left, in the Buddha's description?
o: equanimity, mindfulness, and quiet pleasure in the body
games.why: joy fades, and what's left is equanimous, mindful and pleasant: the lotus soaked in cool water.

practice: Don't look for anything bright; let the breath be ordinary, and notice whether there's any plain, quiet okayness in the body, not excitement, just enough.
If thoughts come, let them pass like ripples on the surface overhead, while you stay below, cool and still.

wordCard.voice: Upekkha, equanimity. The bubbling joy fades and a quiet, mindful ease remains, like a lotus soaked in cool water from root to tip.

orig.note: Pali upekkhā: equanimity, literally looking on; it comes forward in the third jhāna.

carryVoice: Your line: the lotus under water. Thriving, with nothing showy about it. Day three hundred ninety-eight, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the lotus pond simile)
